opening.headline: Learn how to separately design where data is processed and stored and who holds the encryption keys.
body: Suppose your customer contract includes a clause stating that personal data will only be processed within a specified country. AI requests may be processed in multiple regions due to response speed and capacity, so it cannot be said that this provision has been complied with simply by checking the storage location.

In this lesson, we'll break it down into three layers: request receiving, inference, and storage. We then explore the regional options, cross-region inference, and customer-managed keys (CMEK, EKM, key import) offered by the three providers and data platforms, and practice determining what the cost of increased control is.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the concepts of data residency, local processing, and customer management keys
Analyze where cross-region inferences and residency requirements conflict

screens.title: Requirements to be processed only within a specific country
screens.lead: Read one of the contract clauses and consider what this sentence actually requires.

visual.alt: A flow chart with request receipt, inference, and storage divided into three sections, each with a different region label.

paragraphs: There is a provision in the customer contract that personal data will only be processed within a designated country. This service sends AI requests to an external provider. At this time, what should you look for to make sure you are complying with the provisions?

AI requests may be distributed across multiple regions due to response speed and capacity. So we cannot assume that where it is stored and where it is processed is the same. Storage location and processing (inference) location are not the same thing. Where the request comes in, where the model computes, and where the results end up can all be different.

Added to this is the height issue. Even if data is encrypted, the degree of control depends on who holds the encryption keys. If the keys are managed by the provider, you must rely on the provider's operating procedures. If the keys are managed by the customer, you can withdraw the keys and lose access. Control of location and control of height are two different issues.
The questions for this class are: What options will be used to design location and key control?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Does keeping data within one country mean storage or processing? When reading the contract text, start by asking this question.

screens.lead: If you think about the question yourself first and then make a choice, the summary will unfold. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have your customers or regulators ever asked you which country your data is located in?
items.answer: These questions are often answered only by storage location. However, the person asking the question may wonder where it is being processed. The first step is to ask what position means. If you have an answer prepared, you can provide a grounded explanation in contract negotiations.

items.prompt: Do you remember seeing the region selection screen in the cloud console?
items.answer: Region is a setting that selects the geographic location where your service runs and your data is placed. If you leave the defaults, your processing may occur in the region determined by your service provider. It's common to pass by without checking what the default is.

items.prompt: Have you ever checked whether your encryption keys are managed by you or a service provider?
items.answer: In the default setup, the provider typically manages the keys. The option for customers to directly control their keys must be turned on separately, and there are restrictions on the order and scope of turning it on. We address that constraint specifically later in this lesson.
It is not recorded. These are thought-provoking questions and will not be submitted or graded.

screens.title: Where do data residency requirements come from?
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to determine whether the residency requirement comes from law or contract. Depending on the source, how essential the request is and whether there is room for adjustment will vary.

data.caption: Four Sources of Residence Needs
rows: EU GDPR Chapter 5 (Articles 44 to 50)

This involves transferring personal data to a country outside the EU. Transfers to countries with an adequacy decision may be made without separate approval (Article 45); if not, appropriate safeguards, such as standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules adopted by the Commission, are required (Articles 46, 47). Article 49 provides for exceptions in individual circumstances.
It is not a rule that data must be kept within the EU, but rather a condition that must be met when leaving the EU. So, the question arises whether there are grounds for relocation.
Article 28-8 of the Korean Personal Information Protection Act

This involves providing, processing, or storing personal information overseas. In principle, it is prohibited, but it is permitted if one of the following is met: separate consent, special provisions of law or treaty, entrustment of processing and storage for contract performance (if statutory matters are notified), certification notified by the Protection Commission, and recognition that the level of protection is equal.
Processing AI requests on overseas servers or entrusting them to overseas providers can also be transfers, making the location of processing a legal issue.
Laws and supervisory guidelines by sector (home)
Depending on the field, such as finance, medicine, or the public sector, there may be regulations that require data to be kept domestically or to restrict access to data.

Since the intensity of requirements varies from field to field, you should check with your legal representative to see if there are any regulations applicable to your industry. This screen does not list specific regulations.
contract with customer
The customer writes down conditions in the contract, such as processing within a designated country or storage in a specific region.
It is a demand that arises from a contract even if it is not required by law. Unlike legal requirements, there is room to adjust the scope through negotiation.
notes: By distinguishing between residence required by law and residence required by contract, there is a basis for considering whether this requirement is essential or preferred. If it is essential, you must design it while accepting the conflict between model and cost, and if it is a preference, you can compare and negotiate with other options.

Regulations on international transfers are rules that set the conditions for transfer, not rules that unconditionally require domestic storage. If you miss the point that relocation is possible if conditions are met, you are setting up an unnecessarily strong residency requirement.
This table is an overview to understand the structure. Interpretation of specific cases requires review by a legal representative.

screens.title: Two axes of data residency: where to infer and where to store
screens.lead: Switch between the two states, making sure that one setting does not replace the other.

states.label: inference geo
states.body:
The Claude API specifies inference locations on a per-request basis. The default, global, means to infer in any available region for performance and availability reasons, and us means to infer only on US-based infrastructure. There are two values ​​that can be specified: inference_geo can only be used on models that support it, and if specified on a model that does not support it, a 400 error will occur. First check if the model you want to use is in the support list. In the Batch API, values ​​can be given separately for each request.

Organizations can enforce policies by restricting the list of allowed regions and default regions through workspace settings. Since the default region is applied even if the value is omitted in an individual request, this is a device that prevents a developer's mistake from immediately becoming a residency violation.

The usage item in the response will display inference_geo so you can see where the actual processing is located. It's important that you don't just trust the settings, you can verify them with the response. During an audit, keeping this value in the log can show which requests were processed from which region.

states.label: Save location (workspace geo)
states.body:
The storage location determines where data is stored and where endpoint processing, such as image conversion or code execution, occurs. The region value is set when creating a workspace (e.g. us) and cannot be changed later. So before creating a workspace, you need to make sure it meets your contract requirements. Unlike the inference location, which changes on a per-request basis, the storage location is a fixed, workspace-wide choice.

The two settings are independent of each other. Specifying inference as the United States does not automatically cause the storage location to be in the United States, and specifying a storage location does not mean that inference will occur only in that region.

US-only inference, an organization setting on the usage-based Enterprise plan, keeps inference across Claude apps (including background processing like conversation subjects and memory) within the United States, but does not control storage locations and connector services like Slack and Google Drive. Therefore, you should not consider saving as a solution to this single option. You will need to tailor both settings depending on what your contract requires.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen Anthropic's setup, let's follow step-by-step how other platforms pick their locations.

screens.title: Region selection and regional processing options
screens.lead: Follow the step-by-step instructions for locating and using Google's agent platform. Choosing a location may seem like a single click, but it's important to read them in order because they set the standard for everything that follows.

steps.title: Step 1. Choose from supported locations
steps.body: When creating a dataset or importing a model, choose one of the supported locations. In general, it is best to choose a region that is close to your users. If there is a residency requirement, only regions within the requested country are candidates. The platform stores and processes data only in the regions you specify, with the exception of data labeling operations and experimental or preview stage features.

steps.title: Step 2. Check if the desired feature is supported in that region
steps.body: Each feature has different supported regions. Even if you select a region close to you, you will need to select again if the feature you want to use is not available there. Residency requirements narrow the candidate regions, which in turn narrows the range of feature choices.

steps.title: Step 3. Global location is not used
steps.body: This platform does not support the global location for this task. Since the location must be specifically determined, it is a good idea to write down the location in the design document from the beginning.

steps.title: Step 4. Subsequent work will be done in the same location.
steps.body: Once determined, all operations must use the same region as the target resource. If the location is misaligned, resources may not be found or requests may go to unintended locations.

steps.title: Step 5. Specify location in API
steps.body: In the API, you specify regional endpoints (e.g. europe-west4, us-central1) and location values in the resource path. By checking whether this value is fixed in your code or configuration, you can ensure that intent and reality are the same. By including the settings file for review, you can also track who has changed the location.

screens.outro: Choosing a region was a choice within a region. Now let's look at cross-region inference, where the request goes out of region.

screens.title: Cross-region inference and residency requirements
screens.lead: See how what you gain and lose changes as you broaden and narrow the scope of processing. Move the slider to compare how the four benefits change at each point: model selection, throughput, resiliency, and cost. The narrower the scope, the closer it gets to residential needs, but the less advantage there is.

stops.body: Cross-region inference is a feature that automatically directs requests to the region that has capacity. The widest range provides advantages in model selection, throughput, resiliency, and cost. Depending on when and what type of account was created, the default value may be ANY_REGION or it may inherit a cloud region value such as AWS_US. Either way, organizations with residency requirements must check the actual value of their account with SHOW PARAMETERS and specify the value themselves. Although you save only in your account's home region, prompts and responses are temporarily transferred to another region during processing. Credits are calculated as consumed in the requested region and there are no data movement costs.

Like AWS_GLOBAL, AZURE_GLOBAL, and GCP_GLOBAL, requests are sent only within one cloud provider's network, and multiple values can be separated by commas. Although smaller than the entire region, it can still include multiple countries. This step is used when the data needs to stay within the network of a specific cloud provider.

Specify a combination of cloud and geographic region, such as AWS_US, AWS_EU, AZURE_EU, or GCP_US. The advantage is that it can be matched to the area permitted by the contract. Instead, as the scope narrows, the models from which you can choose, processing margins, and resilience decrease.

This is the most restrictive setting, forcing processing only in your account's home region. Use this setting if you have strict residency requirements. In return, you can only use models and features deployed in that region.

There is a distinction to be made at this stage as well. Not storing it and not going through that area are two different demands. Depending on which side your contract language calls for, the options you need will vary.

screens.title: Cryptography Basics: KMS and Envelope Encryption

visual.alt: There is also a two-layer structure in which data is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is wrapped with the parent key of the customer's KMS and stored together.
labels: Parent key (KEK) of the customer KMS
Outside the provider’s system (controlled by the customer)
If withdrawn, decryption is not possible.

screens.lead: Scroll through the step arrows to learn more about what KMS is and why your data is protected with two layers of keys. The CMEK, EKM, and key imports that follow are all built on top of this structure.

steps.title: First, distinguish: during transmission and during storage.
steps.body: Encryption is divided depending on where the data resides. Encryption in transit obscures the content while it passes over the network, while encryption at rest obscures it while it is on disk or in a database. What customer-managed keys primarily address is who holds the keys for encryption at rest. Encryption in transit is a separate protection device.

steps.title: What KMS does
steps.body: Key Management Service (KMS) is a service that creates, stores, and records encryption keys. Encryption and decryption are performed only on authorized calls, and the top-level key never leaves the service's security device in plain text. To use a key, it must go through KMS, so there is a record of who used the key and when.

steps.title: Step 1. Encrypt data with data key
steps.body: Avoid encrypting large data with the top-level key every time. Instead, you create a data key (DEK) to encrypt your data, and then encrypt your data with this key. It is the choice for quickly processing large amounts of data.

steps.title: Step 2. Wrap the data key with a parent key
steps.body: Since the data is decrypted if the data key is left in plaintext, the data key itself is re-encrypted with the parent key (KEK, key encryption key). This wrapped data key is called eDEK. The eDEK can be placed securely next to your encrypted data. This two-layer structure is called envelope encryption.

steps.title: Step 3. When reading, it goes through KMS.
steps.body: To read data, send the eDEK to KMS to request decryption, and unlock the data with the returned data key. The parent key resides only within the customer's KMS, so the provider cannot unlock the data on its own. If the customer revokes the parent key, the eDEK will become unsolvable and the data will no longer be decrypted.

steps.title: Why divide it into two layers?
steps.body: There are two reasons why the AWS KMS documentation explains: The encrypted data key is safe to keep with your data, and when you need to change the protection key, you only need to re-encrypt the small data key rather than the entire larger data. In summary, large-scale processing is handled by the data key, and control is held by the upper key. The control of revocability comes from this parent key.

steps.title: Place the term in this structure
steps.body: CMEK and EKM place the parent key (KEK) in the customer's key service rather than the provider. Key import (BYOK) is a method in which the customer creates the key materials themselves and imports them into KMS. The three terms are not different structures, but a difference in who creates the keys and where they are placed in the same envelope structure. The greater the control of keys, the more operational responsibility for key availability and storage falls on the customer.

screens.outro: Now that we know the key structure, let's read tabbed side by side how both providers provide this structure.

ext.title: AWS KMS Developer Guide, Cryptographic details: envelope encryption

screens.title: Customer Managed Keys: CMEK and EKM
screens.lead: Read the two providers' methods side by side in tabs to see how much control you can have over your keys. The two methods have different terms, but they stand on the same principle that if the customer holds the key, the provider cannot unilaterally release the data. The difference lies in the scope and structure of application.

tabs.label: Anthropic CMEK
tabs.body:
**CMEK** (Customer Managed Encryption Key) is a method of encrypting workspace data at rest using the customer's AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, or Azure Key Vault key. It is optional and eligible organizations can apply to use it. This applies on a per-workspace basis in Claude Platform and on a per-organization basis in Claude Enterprise.

Here's what the customer controls:
- key rotation
- thanks
- Cancel

Since key operations are recorded in the cloud provider's audit log, customers can check who used the key and when.

There are two things to note: Existing data written before the key takes effect will not be re-encrypted. Additionally, some features are turned off or modified when CMEK is turned on. Before adoption, we need to determine which features are affected.

tabs.label: OpenAI EKM
tabs.body:
**EKM** (External Key Management) is a structure that encrypts OpenAI's customer content with keys managed by an external KMS owned by the customer. It can be used in ChatGPT Enterprise and API. Data is encrypted with a data key (DEK), which in turn is encrypted with a key (KEK) in the customer KMS to become an eDEK.

The key point is that KEK is outside of the OpenAI system. The provider cannot unlock the eDEK without the customer's KEK, and therefore cannot decrypt the data.

If the customer withdraws the key, the provider will not be able to decrypt the data. This reversibility is the greatest control that EKM gives. Since eDEK decryption is requested from the customer's KMS for each decryption, if the key service stops, normal use may be blocked, so the availability of the key service also becomes an operational responsibility. Additionally, if you turn on EKM, you will not be able to use beta or alpha features before their official release.

screens.outro: Both methods assume a customer-created key service. You can also choose where to create the key itself, and we'll see how to do that in the next screen.

screens.title: Bringing Keys (BYOK) and Introduction Order
screens.lead: Expand the items one by one to read what key importing solves and what responsibilities it leaves behind. After you've laid out all the items, ask yourself which ones shift responsibility towards the customer.

items.title: something
items.body: AWS KMS provides the ability to create KMS keys without key material and then import customer-generated key material. Since the KMS key is used as key material created by the customer, it is called bring-your-own-key (BYOK).

items.title: Why use it
items.body: Some of the most important reasons for using AWS documentation are as follows. You want to prove that key generation meets your own entropy requirements, you want to utilize existing keys such as code signing or PKI certificate signing, you want to ensure durability and disaster recovery by storing the original outside of AWS, or you want to set an expiration point on the key material and manually delete it so that it can be used again later. It is used in organizations where regulations or internal policies require that you create your own keys.

items.title: Where does the responsibility go?
items.body: Customer is responsible for imported key materials. You can also set the expiration point and manually delete it and use it again. This contrasts with deleting a reservation. Deleted reservations take 7 to 30 days to clear and cannot be restored. Additionally, ciphertext encrypted by AWS KMS cannot be decrypted outside of KMS.

items.title: Introduction order and precautions
items.body: It is recommended that you create a new workspace and associate the key before the request is made. If you attach a key to a workspace that has already received a request, it may take up to a day to be reflected, and previously used data will remain encrypted with a key managed by the provider. Key policies and access subjects should be created with minimum privileges, and key logs should be included in audit procedures.

items.title: Control and operational responsibility
items.body: The higher the level of key control, the greater the customer's operational responsibility. If you lose or accidentally delete your keys, you cannot get your data back. Therefore, procedures such as key backup, access authorization, and expiration notification must be designed together.

screens.title: Commentary: Conflicts between cross-region settings and residency requirements
screens.lead: If your new account defaults to global routing, follow the verification steps: It is important to have the habit of checking the contents of the underlying documents before making a decision at each stage. Writing down what your default, home region, and processing region are is will help you find conflicts quickly. After confirmation, the decision and date will be recorded. Also think about what evidence you need to check at each step.

steps.title: Step 1. check the situation
steps.body: The default for new accounts is regional routing, but the contract has a residency requirement. If you leave the setting as is, your request may be processed in a location that is not permitted by your contract.

steps.title: Step 2. Determine whether the request is for storage or processing
steps.body: First, read whether the contract language restricts only storage locations or processing locations. In a structure where storage is in the account's home region and prompts and responses are temporarily transferred to another region during processing, they are not permanently stored in the processing region. The issue is whether this structure fits the text.

steps.title: Step 3. Narrow your options if you also need to limit processing locations
steps.body: If you need to limit processing locations, narrow your options to Region or DISABLED. The closer you narrow it down, the closer you get to your residential needs, and the less headroom you have in the models and throughput you can use instead.

steps.title: Step 4. Compare available models
steps.body: Verify that narrowing down results in fewer available models against the list of models in the documentation. If the model you were planning to use is missing from the list, you will need to change the design to another model or renegotiate the essentiality of your needs.

steps.title: Step 5. Final check whether the structure matches the contract text
steps.body: Make sure that the structure of storage stays in the home region and is only temporarily transferred during processing matches the contract language. If it is ambiguous, coordinate the wording with your legal representative and record the basis for your decision.

screens.title: Commentary: Read a cross-region setup example
screens.lead: Interpret the extent to which this setting supports the contract's residency requirement. It is not a screen to execute commands, but a screen to read the allowable range indicated by the value. The option names written in the code are different for each provider, but the method of reading the allowable ranges from broad to narrow is the same. Explain for yourself which lines allow for which ranges, and whether those ranges are consistent with the contract language.

notes.note: ANY_REGION is a value that allows requests to be sent to any region that has capacity. Although advantageous for model selection and throughput, it is not suitable for residential needs as the processing area is not fixed.
Specifying a bundle of clouds and regions, such as AWS_US, narrows the allowable range within that. You will need to check whether this bundle matches the territory permitted by your contract.

DISABLED is the most restrictive value, causing processing only in the home region. It should be used when residency requirements are strict, but it must also be taken into account that the new generation model may not be available.

All three lines are settings that determine the processing location rather than saving. This parameter can only be set at the account level and can only be replaced by the ACCOUNTADMIN role. The structure is the same regardless of the value: storage stays in the account home region, prompts and responses are sent temporarily during processing, and are not permanently stored in the processing region.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Let's group the concepts covered in this class into one framework. After reading the three paragraphs above, answer yourself the reflection questions at the end. Your answers will not be recorded or submitted. Reflection questions are intended to help you read in light of your own contracts and services.

paragraphs: Data residency should be defined by dividing request reception, inference, and storage locations. Specifying the storage location alone does not control the processing location; the two settings are independent of each other. Region selection, US-only inference, and cross-region settings are options that primarily control the processing location.

CMEK, EKM, and key import are ways to place control of encryption keys in the hands of the customer. The common core is a structure in which if the customer withdraws the key, the provider will not be able to decrypt the data. However, we must check the limitation that data before introduction may not be the target.

Increasing control creates trade-offs in available models, costs, capabilities, and operational responsibilities. Good design is not about picking the strongest option, but about putting as much control as the contract requires at exactly the right level.
To summarize, the order is to first read what the request refers to, then choose a floor option that fits the request, and finally record the cost of that choice.

glossary.def: Requirements and control over the geographic location where data is stored and processed
How to process inference requests by sending them to another region that has capacity
A method in which the customer encrypts the provider's stored data with his/her KMS key
A structure where the data key is wrapped with the customer KMS key (KEK) and the customer key is required for the provider to decrypt it.
Key material created by the customer is imported into KMS (BYOK)
Data is encrypted with a data key (DEK), and the data key is encrypted again with a parent key (KEK), providing double protection.

misconceptions.myth: Residence is solved by simply specifying a storage location.
misconceptions.fact: The inference processing location must be controlled separately.

misconceptions.myth: If it is cross-region inference, the data is stored in a different country.
misconceptions.fact: There is also a structure of storage in the home region and temporary transmission during processing.

misconceptions.myth: When you turn on CMEK, all historical data is converted to customer keys.
misconceptions.fact: Only data used after the key takes effect is eligible.

misconceptions.myth: Regulations on international transfers mean that personal information must be kept within the country.
misconceptions.fact: Relocation regulations set out the conditions that must be met when moving abroad. Transfer is possible if conditions are met, and strict requirements, such as processing within a designated country, often arise separately from contracts or sector-specific regulations.
